questions.question: How do you reverse a String in Java?
questions.title: How to Reverse a String in Java
questions.direct_answer: The cleanest way is `new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString()`. Alternatively, iterate from the last character to the first and build a new string. For interview problems, `StringBuilder.reverse()` is the expected one-liner; for coding-from-scratch questions, the manual char-swap approach demonstrates understanding of the underlying mechanics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the StringBuilder one-liner and can also implement the manual approach if asked to avoid built-in methods.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to modify the original String character by character — String is immutable, you cannot do that. You must either use StringBuilder or build a new String.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you can also use a char array and swap in place for O(1) extra space. Also cover the palindrome check follow-up: compare the string to its reverse.

sections.title: From Reading Backwards to the One-Line StringBuilder Reverse
sections.content:
At the most basic level, **reversing a String means reading its characters from the last one to the first and gluing them into a new String**. If the input is `"hello"`, you take `'o'`, then `'l'`, `'l'`, `'e'`, `'h'`, and join them into `"olleh"`. That mental model — walk backwards, collect — is the whole algorithm.

The naive way to write that is a loop. Start at `str.length() - 1`, walk down to `0`, and append each `charAt(i)` to a `StringBuilder`. Why a `StringBuilder` and not plain `String` concatenation? Because **`String` is immutable** — every `+` allocates a brand-new String, turning an O(n) job into **O(n²)**. The `StringBuilder` gives you one growable buffer you mutate in place.

Climbing one rung up, you rarely need that loop at all. The JDK ships the idiomatic one-liner: `new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString()`. It wraps the String in a mutable buffer, flips it, and hands back a String — three method calls, **O(n)** time, O(n) space, and the answer an interviewer expects first.

The third rung is the in-place `char[]` swap: call `toCharArray()`, then swap `arr[left]` with `arr[right]`, moving both pointers inward until they meet. Same O(n) time but **O(1)** auxiliary space beyond the array, and it shows you understand two-pointer reversal — the answer when the interviewer bans `StringBuilder`.

The gotcha that separates a fresher from someone who has shipped Java: a hand-rolled character swap breaks on **Unicode surrogate pairs** (emoji and some CJK characters occupy two `char` units). `StringBuilder.reverse()` actually handles surrogate pairs correctly; a manual swap does not unless you account for them. For ASCII interview inputs it never bites, but naming it is the detail that lands.

sections.title: The Steps Behind a Reverse
sections.content:
Every reversal follows the same shape: guard the trivial cases, wrap the text in a mutable buffer, flip it, and return a String.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input String s"] --> B{"s null or length below 2?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["Return s unchanged"]
    B -->|No| D["Wrap s in a StringBuilder"]
    D --> E["Reverse the buffer in place"]
    E --> F["Convert buffer back to String"]
    F --> G["Return the reversed String"]
```

The manual `char[]` swap replaces the middle two boxes with a two-pointer loop, but the guard at the top and the return at the bottom stay the same.

sections.title: All Three Approaches
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trying to mutate the original `String`** — `String` is immutable, so there is no method to change a character in place; reaching for an in-place edit is the classic beginner error. Use a `StringBuilder` or a `char[]` instead.
- **Concatenating with `+` inside a loop** — `result += s.charAt(i)` looks harmless but allocates a fresh `String` every iteration, making the whole thing **O(n²)**. Append to a `StringBuilder` instead.
- **Off-by-one in the manual loop or swap** — starting the index at `s.length()` instead of `length() - 1` throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`; using `while (left <= right)` re-swaps the middle character on odd-length strings. The correct bound is `left < right`.
- **Assuming character reversal is Unicode-safe** — a hand-rolled `char[]` swap corrupts surrogate pairs (emoji, some CJK). `StringBuilder.reverse()` handles them correctly, which is why it is the safer default.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString()`** — the interview-preferred one-liner; **O(n)** time, O(n) space, and it correctly handles Unicode surrogate pairs.
- **`String` is immutable** — you can never reverse in place; every approach builds a new character sequence via `StringBuilder` or a `char[]`.
- **Never use `+` in a loop** — string concatenation in a loop is **O(n²)** because each `+` allocates a new `String`; append to a `StringBuilder` instead.
- **Two-pointer `char[]` swap** — `toCharArray()`, swap `arr[left]`/`arr[right]` inward — **O(1)** auxiliary space, the answer when `StringBuilder` is banned.
- **Edge cases** — guard `null` (otherwise `NullPointerException`) and treat empty or single-character strings as already reversed.
- **Palindrome follow-up** — `str.equals(new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString())` reuses the exact same call.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd reach for the built-in first: `new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString()`. You wrap the String in a mutable buffer, flip it, and turn it back into a String. It's one line, it's **O(n)** in time and space, and it's what most interviewers want to hear — so I'd say it, then offer to do it by hand if they want the mechanics.

If they ban `StringBuilder`, I'd switch to a two-pointer swap on a `char[]`. Convert with `toCharArray()`, put one pointer at the start and one at the end, swap them, and move both inward until they cross. That's still **O(n)** time but **O(1)** extra space, which is the better answer when they're probing for space efficiency. The thing I'd watch is the loop bound — `while (left < right)`, not `<=`, otherwise on an odd-length string you swap the middle character with itself and waste a step.

For edge cases I'd guard `null` so I don't hit a `NullPointerException`, and note that an empty or single-character string is already its own reverse. One detail to stand out: a manual reversal breaks on Unicode surrogate pairs like emoji, but `StringBuilder.reverse()` handles them correctly — so the built-in isn't just shorter, it's safer.

questions.question: How do you count the frequency of each character in a String in Java?
questions.title: Count Character Frequency in a String
questions.direct_answer: Use a `HashMap<Character, Integer>` to store each character as a key and its count as the value. Iterate through the string with `charAt(i)`, and for each character either put it in the map with count 1 or increment the existing count using `getOrDefault()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can use HashMap for frequency counting — this pattern appears in dozens of string and array problems.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a nested loop (O(n²)) to count each character. The HashMap approach is O(n).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the int[26] array approach for lowercase-only strings — O(1) space by using char - 'a' as an index. Also mention that this exact pattern is used in anagram checking: two strings are anagrams if their frequency maps are equal.

sections.title: From Tally Marks to a One-Pass Frequency Map
sections.content:
At the simplest level, **counting character frequency is just keeping a running tally** — one counter per distinct character — as you scan the String from left to right. Read `'a'`, bump its counter; read another `'a'`, bump it again. When you reach the end, each counter holds how many times its character appeared.

The natural Java home for "a counter per key" is a `HashMap<Character, Integer>`. You loop once with `charAt(i)` and, for each character, do `freq.put(c, freq.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1)`. The `getOrDefault(c, 0)` is the trick: it returns the current count, or `0` for a character you have not seen yet, so you always have a number to add one to — no null check, no "is it the first time?" branch. One pass means **O(n)** time, and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters.

A junior reflex is to write a nested loop — pick a character, then scan the whole string counting matches. That is **O(n²)** and the single most common mistake on this question. The map turns it into one clean pass.

Climbing the last rung, when the input is guaranteed lowercase `a`–`z`, you can drop the map entirely and use an `int[26]`. Index each character with `c - 'a'` (so `'a'` maps to `0`, `'z'` to `25`) and increment. That is **O(1)** fixed space, no boxing of `char` into `Character`, and noticeably faster — the optimization worth mentioning.

The gotcha: `int[26]` quietly **assumes ASCII lowercase**. The moment the input has uppercase, digits, spaces, or any Unicode, `c - 'a'` goes out of bounds or collides. For mixed input, fall back to the `HashMap`, and decide up front whether case and whitespace should count toward the tally.

sections.title: One Pass, One Counter Per Character
sections.content:
The whole algorithm is a single loop that looks each character up in the map and writes back its count plus one.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input String s"] --> B["Create empty HashMap"]
    B --> C{"More characters left?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Read next char c"]
    D --> E["Look up current count, default 0"]
    E --> F["Store count plus one for c"]
    F --> C
    C -->|No| G["Map holds each char and its frequency"]
```

For a lowercase-only string the `HashMap` box becomes an `int[26]` and the lookup becomes `count[c - 'a']++`, but the single-pass shape is identical.

sections.title: HashMap Approach and int[26] Approach
HashMap vs int[26] for Frequency Counting
sections.content:
| | `HashMap<Character, Integer>` | `int[26]` array |
|---|---|---|
| Works for | Any Unicode characters | Lowercase a–z only |
| Space complexity | O(k) where k = unique chars | O(1) — always 26 integers |
| Time complexity | O(n) | O(n) |
| Boxing overhead | Yes — char → Character | None — plain int array |
| Readability | Clear intent | Compact but less readable |
| Use when | General purpose, mixed chars | Only lowercase letters |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using a nested loop** — picking each character and rescanning the whole string to count it is **O(n²)**; a single pass with a `HashMap` (or `int[26]`) is **O(n)** and the only acceptable answer.
- **Assuming ASCII with `int[26]`** — `count[c - 'a']` silently goes out of bounds or collides the moment the input has uppercase, digits, spaces, or Unicode. Use `int[26]` only when the input is guaranteed lowercase `a`–`z`; otherwise use a `HashMap`.
- **Forgetting `getOrDefault`** — `freq.put(c, freq.get(c) + 1)` throws a `NullPointerException` the first time it sees a character because `get` returns `null`, which unboxes to nothing. Use `getOrDefault(c, 0)` or `merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)`.
- **Not deciding how case and whitespace count** — treating `'A'` and `'a'` as the same, or ignoring spaces, is a requirements question; clarify and normalize with `toLowerCase()` up front rather than assuming.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`freq.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1`** — the standard one-pass increment; returns `0` for an unseen character so there is never a `NullPointerException` to handle.
- **One pass, O(n) time** — never use a nested loop; frequency counting is the textbook **O(n²)**-to-**O(n)** fix with a map.
- **`int[26]` for lowercase only** — index by `c - 'a'` for **O(1)** fixed space and no `char`-to-`Character` boxing; out of bounds for anything outside `a`–`z`.
- **Edge cases** — decide whether case and whitespace count, normalize with `toLowerCase()`, and handle empty strings (empty map) and `null` explicitly.
- **Anagram reuse** — two strings are anagrams iff their frequency maps (or `int[26]` count arrays) are identical; same pattern, no new idea.
- **First non-repeating character** — build the map in one pass, then a second pass returns the first character whose count is `1`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd build a frequency map in a single pass. Take a `HashMap<Character, Integer>`, walk the string once with `charAt`, and for each character do `freq.put(c, freq.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1)`. The `getOrDefault` is what makes it clean — it hands back `0` the first time it sees a character, so there's no null check and no special first-time branch. That's **O(n)** time and O(k) space, where k is the number of distinct characters.

The mistake I'd explicitly avoid is the nested loop — picking a character and rescanning the whole string to count it. That's **O(n²)** and there's no reason for it once you have the map.

If the interviewer says the input is only lowercase letters, I'd switch to an `int[26]` and index with `c - 'a'`. That drops it to **O(1)** fixed space, skips boxing `char` into `Character`, and runs faster — but I'd call out that it assumes ASCII lowercase, so anything with uppercase, digits, or Unicode goes out of bounds and I'd go back to the map. For edge cases I'd clarify whether case and spaces count and normalize with `toLowerCase()` first. The reason this question shows up so often is the pattern itself — the same frequency map is how you check anagrams and find the first non-repeating character.

questions.question: How do you check if two Strings are anagrams in Java?
questions.title: Anagram Check in Java
questions.direct_answer: Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters the same number of times. The cleanest approaches: sort both strings and compare — `Arrays.sort(s1.toCharArray())` equals `Arrays.sort(s2.toCharArray())`; or build a frequency count and check all counts reach zero.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know at least two approaches and can reason about their time-space trade-offs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking if the same letters appear without checking counts — 'aab' and 'abb' have the same letters but different frequencies, they are NOT anagrams.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare the two approaches: sort is O(n log n) but very short; frequency count is O(n) and better for large strings. Also mention that the frequency counter approach generalises directly to the sliding-window anagram search problem.

sections.title: From Same Letters to a One-Array Frequency Check
sections.content:
At the most basic level, **two strings are anagrams when one is just the other's letters rearranged** — same characters, each appearing the same number of times. `"listen"` and `"silent"` qualify; `"hello"` and `"world"` do not. The simplest way to test that is to **sort both strings and check whether they come out identical** — if shuffling the letters can make them match, sorting lines them up the same way.

The first guard, before any sorting, is length: if the two strings differ in length they cannot possibly be anagrams, so return `false` immediately and skip the work.

The sort approach is short and obvious: `toCharArray()` on each, `Arrays.sort()` both, then `Arrays.equals()`. It is **O(n log n)** because of the sort, and it allocates two new arrays. For an interview that wants the cleanest readable answer, this is fine.

Climbing up, the optimal solution is a single frequency counter. Use one `int[26]`, **increment** for every character in the first string and **decrement** for every character in the second. If the strings are anagrams every bucket nets back to `0`; if any bucket is non-zero, they are not. That is **O(n)** time and **O(1)** space with one array and two passes — better than sorting for large inputs, and it is the exact structure the sliding-window "find all anagrams in a string" problem is built on.

The gotcha that traps candidates: **same letters is not the same as same counts**. `"aab"` and `"abb"` share the letters `a` and `b` but are not anagrams, so a set-based "do the same letters appear?" check is wrong — you must compare frequencies. Also decide up front whether case and spaces matter; `"Dormitory"` vs `"Dirty room"` only works after you lowercase and strip whitespace first.

sections.title: The Frequency-Counter Decision Path
sections.content:
The optimal check guards on length, builds one counter, then verifies every bucket nets to zero.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Strings s1 and s2"] --> B{"Lengths equal?"}
    B -->|No| C["Return false"]
    B -->|Yes| D["Create int array of size 26"]
    D --> E["Increment count for each char in s1"]
    E --> F["Decrement count for each char in s2"]
    F --> G{"Any count not zero?"}
    G -->|Yes| H["Return false — not anagrams"]
    G -->|No| I["Return true — anagrams"]
```

The sort approach collapses the middle into two `Arrays.sort()` calls plus one `Arrays.equals()`, but the length guard at the top is identical and just as important.

sections.title: Both Approaches Side by Side
Sort vs Frequency Counter
sections.content:
| | Sort approach | Frequency counter |
|---|---|---|
| Time complexity | O(n log n) | O(n) |
| Space complexity | O(n) — new char arrays | O(1) — fixed 26-element array |
| Code length | ~4 lines | ~6 lines |
| Handles Unicode? | Yes | Only a–z (use HashMap for Unicode) |
| Extends to sliding window? | No | Yes — core of anagram-in-string search |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Checking letters, not counts** — verifying that the same distinct letters appear (a `Set` comparison) wrongly reports `"aab"` and `"abb"` as anagrams. You must compare how many times each character appears, not just which characters exist.
- **Skipping the length guard** — without the early `s1.length() != s2.length()` check you do needless work, and a sloppy comparison of different-length inputs can even mask a bug. Bail out first.
- **Hard-coding `int[26]` for any input** — like frequency counting, `c - 'a'` assumes lowercase `a`–`z`. For Unicode, case-sensitive, or mixed input, use a `HashMap<Character, Integer>` instead.
- **Ignoring case and spaces in phrase anagrams** — `"Dormitory"` and `"Dirty room"` are anagrams only after you lowercase and strip whitespace; failing to normalize gives a wrong `false`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Length guard first** — different lengths means not anagrams; return `false` before sorting or counting.
- **Sort approach** — `Arrays.sort()` both `char[]`s and compare with `Arrays.equals()`; **O(n log n)**, ~4 lines, the most readable answer.
- **Frequency counter** — one `int[26]`, `++` for s1 and `--` for s2, then check every bucket is `0`; **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space, better for large inputs.
- **Same letters ≠ same counts** — `"aab"` and `"abb"` share letters but differ in frequency, so they are NOT anagrams; never check with a `Set`.
- **Unicode / case** — `int[26]` assumes lowercase `a`–`z`; use a `HashMap<Character, Integer>` for the full charset, and normalize case and spaces for phrase anagrams.
- **Generalizes to sliding window** — the counter is the core of "find all anagrams of a pattern in a string" — an **O(n)** substring search.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd start with the cheap guard: if the two strings are different lengths, they can't be anagrams, so return `false` immediately. After that I've got two approaches.

The simple one is sort and compare — `toCharArray()` on both, `Arrays.sort()` each, then `Arrays.equals()`. If shuffling could make them match, sorting lines them up identically. It's about four lines and very readable, but the sort makes it **O(n log n)** and it allocates two arrays.

The one I'd reach for when complexity matters is a single frequency counter. One `int[26]`: increment for every character in the first string, decrement for every character in the second. If they're anagrams every bucket lands back on `0`; any non-zero bucket means no. That's **O(n)** time and **O(1)** space.

The trap I'd make sure to avoid out loud is treating 'same letters' as 'same counts' — `"aab"` and `"abb"` have the same letters but different frequencies, so they're not anagrams; a `Set` check gets that wrong. For edge cases, `int[26]` assumes lowercase `a`–`z`, so for Unicode or mixed case I'd use a `HashMap` and normalize case and spaces first. One thing that stands out: that same counter is exactly what the sliding-window 'find all anagrams' problem is built on.
